description: Standardized core culinary techniques catalog structured for in-app micro-tutorials, visual looping previews, and step-by-step cooking mode callouts.

techniques.name: Pan Searing Protein
techniques.summary: Cooking protein at high temperature in a hot pan to trigger the Maillard reaction, developing a deeply flavorful, caramelized brown crust.
key_tips: Thoroughly pat the protein completely dry with paper towels; surface moisture causes steaming rather than browning.
Ensure the pan and oil are shimmering hot before the protein touches the metal.
Do not move or poke the meat for the first 3-5 minutes; it will naturally release from the pan once the crust forms.
common_mistakes: Crowding the pan, which drops thermal temperature and traps steam.
Flipping prematurely when meat is still adhering to the pan.
Using low-smoke-point fats (like extra virgin olive oil or unclarified butter) at scorching heat.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Close-up slow motion of dried steak entering shimmering oil; golden crust formation; natural clean release with tongs.

techniques.name: Deglazing a Pan
techniques.summary: Pouring a cool liquid (wine, broth, vinegar, or water) into a hot pan after searing to dissolve and incorporate the caramelized browned food particles (fond) stuck to the bottom.
key_tips: Pour liquid in immediately after removing meat while pan retains thermal heat.
Use a flat-edged wooden spoon to aggressively scrape the bottom until smooth.
Reduce liquid by at least 50% to concentrate sweetness and cook off harsh alcohol fumes.
common_mistakes: Deglazing a pan with burnt (blackened) fond, which infuses an acrid, bitter taste into the sauce.
Adding liquid when the pan has cooled down completely.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Wine hitting hot skillet; sudden steam burst; flat wooden spoon scraping fond into a rich amber liquid.

techniques.name: Braising (Low & Slow)
techniques.summary: A combination cooking method where meat/vegetables are first seared at high heat, then slowly simmered partially submerged in flavorful liquid in a covered vessel at low heat.
key_tips: Liquid should come roughly 1/3 to 1/2 way up the side of the meat, never fully submerged.
Keep the oven temperature low (300°F / 150°C) to gently melt tough collagen into succulent gelatin without drying out muscle fibers.
Keep lid tightly sealed to prevent steam evaporation.
common_mistakes: Boiling too rapidly, which toughens the protein and turns sauce greasy.
Skipping the initial deep browning sear.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Lid lifting off Dutch oven; gentle slow bubbles breaking around tender braised short ribs; fork-tender pull.

techniques.name: Julienne Cut (Matchstick)
techniques.summary: Precision knife technique that cuts firm vegetables into uniform matchsticks measuring approximately 1/8 inch x 1/8 inch x 2 inches (3mm x 3mm x 5cm).
key_tips: Square off the vegetable first by cutting a thin slice off one side so it rests stable without rolling.
Cut into 1/8-inch thick planks, stack 2-3 planks, and slice lengthwise into 1/8-inch sticks.
Always curl non-knife hand fingertips inward like a claw against the blade face.
common_mistakes: Attempting to cut round vegetables without squaring a flat base first.
Uneven stick thicknesses causing erratic cooking rates in stir-fries.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Claw grip demonstration; fluid rhythmic knife slice through carrot planks; perfect matchsticks fanning out.

techniques.name: Chiffonade (Herb Ribbons)
techniques.summary: Slicing flat leafy greens or herbs (such as fresh basil, sage, or mint) into thin, delicate ribbons.
key_tips: Stack 6-8 washed and thoroughly dried leaves from largest to smallest.
Roll the leaf stack tightly like a cigar.
Slice crosswise into thin 1/16-inch ribbons using a smooth single-pass slicing motion.
common_mistakes: Using a dull knife or pressing straight down, which bruises and blackens the cut edges of delicate basil leaves.
Chiffonading wet herbs, resulting in clumps.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Tightly rolled basil leaves; clean crosswise strokes; green ribbons separating effortlessly.

techniques.name: Emulsification (Sauce Binding)
techniques.summary: Forcing two naturally unmixable liquids (such as oil and water or vinegar) to combine into a stable, silky uniform suspension using a binding agent like egg yolk, mustard, or honey.
key_tips: Add the oil very slowly—drop by drop initially—while whisking vigorously until the emulsion takes hold.
Ensure base ingredients (egg yolk, acid) are at room temperature.
If an emulsion breaks (separates into greasy curdles), whisk 1 tsp warm water in a clean bowl and slowly whisk the broken sauce into it.
common_mistakes: Pouring oil too quickly in a steady stream before the initial emulsion matrix forms.
Using ice-cold liquids which inhibit surfactant binding.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Thin stream of oil drizzling into egg yolk and Dijon; rapid whisking; glossy, thick mayonnaise forming.

techniques.name: Tempering Delicate Ingredients
techniques.summary: Gently raising the temperature of cold, heat-sensitive ingredients (such as beaten eggs, yogurt, or sour cream) before adding them to hot mixtures to prevent curdling or scrambling.
key_tips: Slowly ladle a small stream of the hot soup/broth into the eggs/dairy while constantly whisking.
Once the egg/dairy mixture is lukewarm to warm, pour it steadily back into the main pot while stirring.
Keep main pot at low heat; do not boil after incorporating tempered eggs.
common_mistakes: Dumping cold egg yolks or sour cream directly into boiling soup.
Failing to whisk continuously during the tempering pour.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Ladle of hot broth poured into glass bowl of whisked eggs; continuous whisk; warmed mixture poured back into saucepan.

techniques.name: Blanching and Shocking
techniques.summary: Boiling vegetables briefly in heavily salted water, then immediately plunging them into an ice water bath to stop the cooking instantly.
key_tips: Use abundant rolling boiling water (at least 4 quarts per pound of vegetables) heavily salted like sea water.
Boil only until crisp-tender (60-90 seconds for green beans, asparagus, or peas).
Keep the ice bath properly iced so it remains near 32°F (0°C).
common_mistakes: Leaving vegetables in the ice bath too long after they have cooled, which leaches flavor and nutrients.
Inadequate ice volume, which warms up into a lukewarm bath that continues overcooking.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Vibrant green asparagus lifted with tongs from boiling water; submerged in clear ice bath; brilliant color lock.

techniques.name: Sweating Aromatics
techniques.summary: Cooking chopped vegetables (onions, celery, carrots, leeks) in fat over low heat with salt, softening them and releasing their natural moisture without browning.
key_tips: Keep heat strictly on low to medium-low.
Add fine salt immediately to draw out cellular moisture via osmosis.
Cover pan with lid or parchment paper cartouche to trap steam and encourage even softening.
common_mistakes: Allowing heat to climb until vegetables brown, which imparts caramelized notes rather than sweet, translucent base aromatics.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Translucent diced onions simmering gently in butter; zero golden browning; soft glossy texture.

techniques.name: Folding Delicate Batters
techniques.summary: A gentle motion used to incorporate a light, airy ingredient (whipped egg whites or whipped cream) into a heavier batter without deflating the trapped air bubbles.
key_tips: Use a flexible rubber spatula with a broad head.
Cut vertically down through the center of the mixture, sweep across the bottom of the bowl, and lift up along the side, rotating the bowl 90 degrees.
Stir in one-third of the light mixture first to lighten the base before gently folding the rest.
common_mistakes: Vigorous circular stirring, which collapses delicate foam bubbles and produces dense, flat cakes.
Under-folding leaving large unmixed streaks of raw egg white.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Spatula cutting down center of chocolate batter; sweeping under whipped egg whites and rolling over; airy texture maintained.

techniques.name: Resting Cooked Meat
techniques.summary: Allowing cooked meat to sit undisturbed on a warm cutting board before slicing, allowing muscle fibers to relax and redistribute moisture throughout.
key_tips: Rest steaks for 5-8 minutes; whole roasted chickens for 15 minutes; large roasts for 20-30 minutes.
Tent loosely with foil—never wrap tightly, which creates condensation and softens crisp skin or sear.
Save all residual cutting board juices and pour back over the sliced meat or whisk into pan gravy.
common_mistakes: Slicing meat straight off the grill or pan, causing high-pressure juices to flood out, leaving meat dry.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Juicy steak resting on wooden board; slice revealing edge-to-edge pink interior with juices retained inside cell walls.

techniques.name: Monter au Beurre (Pan Sauce Gloss)
techniques.summary: Whisking chilled cubes of unsalted butter into a simmering, reduced pan sauce off the heat to create a glossy, velvety consistency and rich mouthfeel.
key_tips: Butter must be straight from the refrigerator (ice cold) and cubed.
Remove the pan from direct heat; residual heat melts butter slowly, maintaining the natural dairy emulsion.
Swirl pan constantly in a circular motion until butter is fully emulsified.
common_mistakes: Boiling the sauce while adding butter, which breaks the emulsion into a pool of yellow clarified oil.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Cold cube of butter dropped into dark wine reduction off heat; pan swirling; sauce transforming to high-gloss sheen.

techniques.name: Gentle Poaching
techniques.summary: Submerging delicate foods (eggs, fish, pears) in liquid maintained at a gentle sub-boil (160°F–180°F / 71°C–82°C) with tiny shivers instead of rolling bubbles.
key_tips: Water should have faint convection currents and tiny bubbles pinned to the bottom of the pot.
For poached eggs: add 1 tbsp white vinegar, create a gentle vortex in the water, and slip egg from a small ramekin directly into center.
Use aromatic liquid (court-bouillon or seasoned broth) to infuse flavor.
common_mistakes: Allowing liquid to reach a rapid boil, which rips delicate egg whites apart and dries out fish proteins.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Gentle water swirl; egg dropping in; whites wrapping neatly around yolk in tranquil simmering water.

techniques.name: Dry Brining
techniques.summary: Salting meat in advance and letting it rest uncovered on a wire rack in the refrigerator for 4 to 24 hours, enhancing juiciness and promoting razor-crisp skin.
key_tips: Use approximately 1/2 tsp kosher salt per pound of meat.
Rest on an elevated wire cooling rack inside a sheet pan to allow air circulation completely around.
Do not cover; the dry refrigerator air dehydrates the skin surface for superior Maillard browning.
common_mistakes: Using fine table salt at the same volume as kosher salt, which severely oversalts the meat.
Rinsing the meat after brining (unnecessary and washes away absorbed seasoning).

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Salt crystals dissolving into steak surface; translucent dry skin glistening under cool air.

techniques.name: True Onion Caramelization
techniques.summary: Slowly cooking sliced onions over low-to-medium heat for 40-50 minutes until their natural sugars break down into complex, sweet, deeply golden-brown compounds.
key_tips: Patience is non-negotiable; true caramelization cannot be rushed in 10 minutes without burning.
Add a pinch of salt initially to draw out water.
Splash 1-2 tbsp water, wine, or stock whenever the fond on the bottom gets too dark to redistribute sugars.
common_mistakes: High heat causing onions to char bitter black on tips before interior sugars break down.
Adding baking soda excessively, which makes onions mushy and chemically alkaline.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Time-lapse transition: raw pale sliced onions -> soft yellow -> golden -> deep mahogany brown onion jam.

techniques.name: Blooming Spices in Fat
techniques.summary: Frying ground or whole spices in warm oil or ghee for 30–60 seconds, which dissolves and amplifies their fat-soluble aromatic flavor compounds (tadka / tempering).
key_tips: Heat fat over medium-low heat; spices burn easily.
Add whole seeds (cumin, mustard, coriander) first until they crackle and pop, then ground spices for 15-20 seconds.
Add wet aromatics (onion, garlic, ginger) or liquids immediately after blooming to arrest spice cooking.
common_mistakes: Dumping ground spices into boiling water/soup directly without fat blooming, resulting in raw, dusty flavor.
Burning delicate ground paprika or turmeric into bitter black residue.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Mustard seeds popping in hot ghee; fragrant ground turmeric and cumin blooming with aromatic bubbles.

techniques.name: Making a Roux
techniques.summary: Cooking equal parts by weight of fat (usually butter) and all-purpose flour to eliminate raw flour taste and create the foundational thickening base for mother sauces.
key_tips: White roux (2 min) for Béchamel / mac and cheese.
Blond roux (4-5 min) for Velouté / chicken pot pie.
Brown or Dark roux (15-30 min) for Creole and Cajun gumbo.
Whisk liquid in gradually—hot liquid into warm roux, or cold liquid into hot roux—to prevent lumping.
common_mistakes: Adding liquid all at once, creating stubborn flour dumplings.
Under-cooking white roux, resulting in an unpleasant pasty flour flavor.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Melted butter whisking with flour into a foaming paste; transitioning from pale cream to golden blond.

techniques.name: Supreming Citrus
techniques.summary: Cutting raw citrus fruit segments cleanly away from the bitter peel, white pith, and fibrous membrane walls.
key_tips: Slice off both top and bottom ends of orange/grapefruit so it stands flat.
Curve your chef knife or paring knife along the contour of the fruit, cutting away skin and all white pith.
Slice inward on each side of the white dividing membranes to release clean, perfect fruit segments.
common_mistakes: Leaving patches of bitter white pith on fruit edges.
Squeezing fruit with excessive hand pressure while cutting.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Curving knife removing skin and pith; precision blade sliding between membrane walls to drop jewel-like segment.

techniques.name: Sous Vide & Reverse Sear
techniques.summary: Cooking vacuum-sealed food in a precisely controlled water bath to the exact desired core temperature, followed by a blazing 60-second sear to develop crust.
key_tips: Ensure airtight vacuum seal so heat transfers uniformly through water immersion.
Pat exterior bone-dry before the post-bath sear.
Sear on maximum surface heat for no longer than 45-60 seconds per side to avoid cooking beyond the water bath target.
common_mistakes: Searing cold or wet meat from the bag without drying, causing gray band overcooking.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Water circulator bath at 54°C (129°F); steak removed from bag, dried, hitting smoking cast iron for rapid sear.

techniques.name: Blind Baking Pastry Crust
techniques.summary: Pre-baking an empty tart or pie crust before adding wet or unbaked fillings, preventing the bottom crust from turning into a soggy, undercooked mess.
key_tips: Dock (prick) the pastry bottom gently all over with a fork to release trapped air.
Line with crumpled parchment paper and fill completely to the brim with ceramic pie weights, dried beans, or raw rice.
Bake until edges set (15 min), then remove weights and bake 5-10 min more to crisp the floor.
common_mistakes: Skimping on pie weights, which causes crust walls to slump down into the pan.
Adding weights directly onto raw dough without parchment lining.

micro_tutorial_spec.visual_cues: Parchment lining fluted tart shell; dried beans poured in to the brim; baked crust revealed crisp and golden.
